On October 21, 2004, the International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium, led in the United States by the National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI) and the Department of Energy (DOE), published its scientific description of the completed human genome sequence. This work revised the estimated number of human protein-coding genes from 35,000 to a range of 20,000–25,000, a surprisingly low number for our species. The findings were reported in the October 21 issue of Nature. 2. On October 22, 2004, the ENCODE Consortium published a paper in the journal Science outlining the scientific rationale and strategy for its effort to create a comprehensive catalog of all functional elements in the human genome that are crucial to biological processes. 3. On November 8, 2004, the NHGRI partnered with the Department of Health and Human Services and the Office of the Surgeon General to launch a free computer program called My Family Health Portrait. This tool allows the public to record important family health information to help identify common hereditary diseases. 4. On December 8, 2004, the NHGRI and the International Chicken Genome Sequencing Consortium announced the publication of an analysis comparing the chicken and human genomes. This marked the first time a bird's genome had been sequenced and analyzed. The findings were published in the December 9 issue of Nature. 5. On December 10, 2004, the International HapMap Consortium announced the removal of restrictions on data generated from its efforts to map human genetic variation. This decision made all the consortium's data publicly available, facilitating easier access for researchers to tools for identifying genetic contributions to diseases. 6. On February 7, 2005, the International HapMap Consortium announced plans to create a more powerful map of human genetic variation than originally envisioned. This enhanced map aims to accelerate the discovery of genes associated with common diseases such as asthma, cancer, diabetes, and heart disease. 7. On March 16, 2005, as part of the Human Genome Project, the NIH celebrated the first comprehensive analysis of the human X chromosome sequence. This analysis provided groundbreaking insights into the evolution of sex chromosomes and the biological differences between males and females. 8. On August 8, 2005, the NHGRI announced the awarding of grants totaling more than $32 million to advance the development of innovative DNA sequencing technologies. These technologies aim to reduce the cost of DNA sequencing and expand the use of genomics in biomedical research and healthcare. 9. On August 29, 2005, a research team led by the NHGRI discovered that a class of experimental anti-cancer drugs showed promise in laboratory studies for treating a fatal genetic disorder that causes premature aging. 10. On August 31, 2005, the first comprehensive comparison of the genetic blueprints of humans and chimpanzees revealed that our closest living relatives share 96% of our DNA sequence. 11. On October 5, 2005, the NIH announced contracts that would provide researchers with unprecedented access to two private collections of knockout mice. These resources offer valuable models for studying human diseases and lay the groundwork for a public, genome-wide library of knockout mice. 12. On October 26, 2005, the International HapMap Consortium published a comprehensive catalog of human genetic variation. This landmark achievement is already accelerating the search for genes involved in common diseases such as asthma, diabetes, cancer, and heart disease. 13. On November 15, 2005, as part of the U.S. Surgeon General's Family Health Initiative, an updated version of a computerized tool designed to help families gather their health information was unveiled. 14. On December 13, 2005, the National Cancer Institute (NCI) and the NHGRI launched a comprehensive effort to accelerate understanding of the molecular basis of cancer through the application of genome analysis technologies, particularly large-scale genome sequencing. 15. On February 8, 2006, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) announced the creation of two new initiatives aimed at speeding up research into the causes of common diseases such as asthma, arthritis, and Alzheimer’s disease. 16. On March 29, 2006, a multi-institution team of experts, coordinated by NHGRI geneticists, supported efforts to identify more than 70 unidentified bodies in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina. 17. On July 18, 2006, researchers discovered that genetic alterations originally identified in individuals with a rare disease may also be an important risk factor for the second most common form of dementia among the elderly. 18. On July 24, 2006, researchers at the NIH Chemical Genomics Center (NCGC), an NHGRI-affiliated center, developed a new screening approach that profiles compounds in large chemical libraries more accurately and precisely than standard methods. This innovation accelerates the production of data for probing biological activities and identifying leads for drug discovery. 19. On August 21, 2006, the NHGRI, part of the NIH, announced grants totaling $54 million over five years to establish one new Center of Excellence in Genomic Science (CEGS) and continue support for two existing centers. 20. On September 13, 2006, the NCI and NHGRI announced the first three cancers to be studied in the pilot phase of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). The cancers selected for study were lung, brain (glioblastoma), and ovarian cancers. 21. On October 4, 2006, the NHGRI announced the latest round of grant awards totaling more than $13 million to accelerate the development of innovative sequencing technologies. These technologies aim to reduce the cost of DNA sequencing and expand the use of genomics in medical research and healthcare. 22. On October 16, 2006, the NCI and NHGRI announced two additional components of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) Pilot Project, a three-year, $100 million collaboration to test the feasibility of using large-scale genome analysis technologies to identify critical genetic changes involved in cancer. 23. On November 15, 2006, new family health history projects were launched, focusing on Alaska Native and Appalachian communities. These efforts aim to educate all Americans about the importance of knowing their family health histories. 24. On January 15, 2007, scientists discovered a new genetic clue to the cause of Alzheimer’s disease. Variations in a gene known as SORL1 may contribute to the development of late-onset Alzheimer’s disease, according to an international team of researchers. 25. On April 26, 2007, researchers identified new genetic risk factors for type 2 diabetes. In the most comprehensive study of genetic risk factors for type 2 diabetes to date, a U.S.-Finnish team, working closely with two other groups, identified at least four new genetic variants associated with increased diabetes risk and confirmed the existence of another six. 26. On May 4, 2007, the NHGRI and NCI partnered with Group Health Cooperative to advance genomic research.
